The provided web page excerpt is metadata for a journal article titled *"The Evolution of OCR-Free Visual Document Understanding: From Heuristic OCR to End-to-End Multimodal Transformers"*, authored by Aarti Ahirwar and Ritu Tandon, affiliated with SAGE University, India. The article is set to be published in Volume 3, Issue 2 (2026) of the *International Journal of Research and Review in Applied Science, Humanities, and Technology* (ISSN: 3048-975X), and is indexed with DOI: 10.71143/gaza7e33.

**Summary for a Researcher:**

The abstract outlines a shift in Visual Document Understanding (VDU) from traditional OCR-dependent, multi-stage pipelines to OCR-free, end-to-end multimodal transformer models that process raw pixels directly into structured text outputs. It identifies OCR error propagation—where inaccuracies in OCR degrade downstream NLP performance—as a key limitation of prior approaches. The paper reviews the architectural evolution toward OCR-free systems, including Layout-aware Transformers, Vision Transformers (ViT), hierarchical models like Swin, and generative frameworks such as Donut and Pix2Struct. It also discusses core technical challenges, including handling high-resolution document images and achieving effective cross-modal alignment between visual and textual elements. The authors evaluate state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks and suggest future research directions in the context of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs).

We present YOLO, a new approach to object detection. Prior work on object detection repurposes classifiers to perform detection. Instead, we frame object detection as a regression problem to spatially separated bounding boxes and associated class probabilities. A single neural network predicts bounding boxes and class probabilities directly from full images in one evaluation. Since the whole detection pipeline is a single network, it can be optimized end-to-end directly on detection performance. Our unified architecture is extremely fast. Our base YOLO model processes images in real-time at 45 frames per second. A smaller version of the network, Fast YOLO, processes an astounding 155 frames per second while still achieving double the mAP of other real-time detectors. Compared to state-of-the-art detection systems, YOLO makes more localization errors but is less likely to predict false positives on background. Finally, YOLO learns very general representations of objects. It outperforms other detection methods, including DPM and R-CNN, when generalizing from natural images to other domains like artwork.
